cards.explanation: The answer is False. The writer says faith is “…the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.” It's about the things we can't see yet, friends. I don't need faith to know a cookie is on the tray when I'm looking right at it.

The answer is not out of what was visible. The writer says we understand by faith that the universe was formed at God's command, “…so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.” So everything we see didn't come from something we could already see, friends. God spoke and it was formed.

The word is righteous. The writer says Abel “…was commended as righteous when God gave approval to his gifts.” It was by faith, so the commending came from God and not from Abel patting himself on the back. Abel offered a better sacrifice than Cain did, friends.

The answer is True. The writer says that “…by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead.” This is Abel, who offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did. His faith is still talking, all these years later, friends.

The answer is True, and look at the order, friends. The writer says of Enoch, “…before he was taken, he was commended as one who pleased God.” The commending comes first, then the taking up. If that were on my résumé, I'd frame it and hang it right over my ovens.

The two words are exists and rewards, friends. The writer says without faith it's impossible to please God, and anyone who approaches Him “…must believe that He exists…” You can't come to someone you don't believe is there. And that person must believe He “…rewards those who earnestly seek Him.” Notice that it says earnestly. God rewards those who really go looking for Him.

The answer is an ark to save his family. The writer says Noah, “…when warned about things not yet seen, in godly fear built an ark to save his family.” He built it because of what he'd been warned about, friends.

The answer is the righteousness that comes by faith. The writer says Noah “…became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.” That happened by faith, right along with building the ark. By faith, the writer says, he also condemned the world, friends.

The answer is True, friends. The writer says Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, “…obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going.” He couldn't say where he was going, but he still went.
The answer is tents, friends. The writer says Abraham “…lived in tents…” He was in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. Isaac and Jacob lived in tents too.

The word is foundations. The writer says Abraham “…was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.” Think about it, friends: a tent has no foundation at all. He's in tents, but he's looking ahead to a city God designed and built.

The answer is that she considered God faithful to His promise. The writer says Sarah was enabled to conceive “…because she considered Him faithful who had promised.” Her faith rested on the One who made the promise, friends. She was barren and beyond the proper age, and still she counted on Him.

The answer is as many as the stars and the sand. The writer says that from one man, “…and he as good as dead…” came descendants “…as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.” I know a little about stars, friends, because mine light up when a box is done. Nobody is counting these.

The answer is True, friends. The writer says that “…they saw them and welcomed them from afar.” That comes right after the writer says they died without having received the things they were promised. I picture someone waving hard at a bakery window from clear across the street.

The answer is a country of their own. The writer says those who talk this way “…show that they are seeking a country of their own.” They called themselves strangers and exiles on the earth, friends. That tells us they were looking for a home.
The word is heavenly, friends. The writer says, “…they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one.” They didn't long for the country they left. They longed for something better.

The answer is False, friends. The writer says, “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them.” That “Therefore” ties it back to their longing for a heavenly country. I think that's about the warmest line in the whole chapter.
